source: Machado, Bellemare, Bowling (2017) A Laplacian Framework for Option Discovery in RL (ICML)
finding: Proposes eigenpurposes: intrinsic rewards from the eigenvectors of the graph Laplacian (proto-value functions). Each gives an option (eigenoption) that moves the agent along one direction of the state space. No task reward is used, so options are task-independent.
numbers: Tabular tests in an open room, an I-Maze and the 4-room domain; Atari via RAM state (1,024 bits).
limits: Needs a graph or sampled transitions; problem-state graphs for reasoning are not given.
agent_relevance: Options are found from the structure of the state graph, not from rewards. A scaffold could derive subgoals from a graph of problem states without a solved example.

source: Machado, Bellemare, Bowling (2017) A Laplacian Framework for Option Discovery in RL (ICML)
finding: In the 4-room domain the first eigenoptions do NOT end at doorways. The fifth eigenoption is the first to terminate at a doorway entrance. Bottlenecks are not the first thing the Laplacian finds.
numbers: 4-room, I-Maze, open room; deterministic grids, 4 actions.
quote: Doorways are not the first options we discover in the 4-room domain (the fifth eigenoption is the first to terminate at the entrance of a doorway).
limits: Qualitative figure; one small domain.
agent_relevance: Eigen-subgoals are corners, rooms and corridor ends, not only choke points. A bottleneck-only subgoal library would miss them.

source: Machado, Bellemare, Bowling (2017) A Laplacian Framework for Option Discovery in RL (ICML)
finding: New metric: diffusion time, the expected steps to go between two random states under a random walk over primitives plus options. Options are added in order of eigenvalue. The first few options RAISE diffusion time (hurt exploration). Enough options cut it a lot.
numbers: Open room, I-Maze, 4-room; random-walk behaviour policy; options added incrementally by increasing eigenvalue.
limits: Result is for exploration and learning. For planning, options prune the tree, so few options can still help (authors say so).
agent_relevance: A small set of subgoals can be worse than none for exploration. A subgoal library needs enough variety and different timescales before it helps.

source: Machado, Bellemare, Bowling (2017) A Laplacian Framework for Option Discovery in RL (ICML)
finding: With only bottleneck options (go to the nearest doorway), diffusion time in the 4-room domain goes UP. Agents keep moving between rooms and rarely reach outer corners. Eigenoptions work at several timescales and fix this.
numbers: 4-room domain, options each defined inside a room to move to the closest doorway (appendix Fig 10).
limits: Measured by diffusion time (a model metric), not by human or LLM performance.
agent_relevance: Bottleneck-only subgoals can narrow behaviour. Mix near and far subgoals.

source: Machado, Bellemare, Bowling (2017) A Laplacian Framework for Option Discovery in RL (ICML)
finding: Reward accumulation: Q-learning with eigenoptions in the behaviour policy reaches the goal corner faster. Best result with 64 options (32 plus their negations). Performance is fairly robust to the number. Few options can hurt.
numbers: Agent starts bottom-left, goal top-right, reward +1 at goal; Q-learning alpha 0.1, gamma 0.9; 100-step episodes; 250 episodes (10x10 grid, I-Maze) or 500 (4-room); mean of 100 trials.
limits: Small tabular tasks.
agent_relevance: Number of subgoals is a model-selection choice. Plan for pruning weak ones.

source: Machado, Bellemare, Bowling (2017) A Laplacian Framework for Option Discovery in RL (ICML)
finding: Eigenoptions beat bottleneck options when the goal is far from the doorways. When the goal is near a doorway, bottleneck options are competitive. Switching start and goal had no effect on eigenoptions.
numbers: 4-room, 64 eigenoptions vs doorway options, several start/goal pairs (appendix D, Fig 14), 250 episodes, 100 trials.
limits: Authors note 64 eigenoptions may not cover all regions.
agent_relevance: Which subgoal type wins depends on where the goal lies relative to choke points. 'Always bottleneck' is a boundary condition, not a rule.

source: Machado, Bellemare, Bowling (2017) A Laplacian Framework for Option Discovery in RL (ICML)
finding: Control: random options (random state as subgoal) are not competitive. Added in 24 random orders, most sequences RAISE diffusion time by several orders of magnitude until nearly every state has its own option. In some runs the agent never learns to reach the goal.
numbers: 4-room, 24 random orderings; appendix C, Fig 11.
limits: Tabular.
agent_relevance: Subgoals must be structured. Random subgoals can be worse than none.

source: Machado, Bellemare, Bowling (2017) A Laplacian Framework for Option Discovery in RL (ICML)
finding: Sample-based version: collect transitions as differences of feature vectors into an incidence matrix T, then SVD. For tabular one-hot features and full coverage it gives the same options as the combinatorial Laplacian. Used on Atari RAM (25,000 sampled rows, 1,024 bits).
numbers: Atari 2600 via ALE; options approximated with one-step look-ahead; six predefined start states per game; at least 25,000 observed transitions per round.
limits: Atari evidence is anecdotal (trajectory plots in Freeway, Montezuma, Ms Pac-Man), no score numbers.
agent_relevance: Shows subgoal discovery can run from raw experience.

source: Machado, Rosenbaum, Guo, Liu, Tesauro, Campbell (2018) Eigenoption Discovery through the Deep Successor Representation (ICLR)
finding: Extends eigenoptions to stochastic transitions and raw pixels by using the deep successor representation (SR) in place of the Laplacian (SR and proto-value functions are equivalent). Tabular: options from SR estimated after 100 episodes cut diffusion time and speed Q-learning; an accurate SR is not needed.
numbers: Rooms domain; Q-learning alpha 0.1, gamma 0.9, 100-step episodes; mean of 24 independent SR-learning runs, each with 100 Q-learning runs.
quote: a very accurate estimate of the successor representation is not necessary for the eigenoptions to be useful
limits: Tabular rooms; sample cost of learning the options is excluded by design.
agent_relevance: SR is a cheap, noise-tolerant source of subgoals; rough structure is enough.

source: Machado, Rosenbaum, Guo, Liu, Tesauro, Campbell (2018) Eigenoption Discovery through the Deep Successor Representation (ICLR)
finding: Atari from pixels: random policy for 50,000 steps, SR stored per state, eigenpurposes from the right singular vectors. In 3 of 4 games (Bank Heist, Montezuma's Revenge, Ms Pac-Man) options push the agent to corners and relevant places. In Montezuma the option end points match known good subgoals (Kulkarni 2016). Failed in Freeway.
numbers: Greedy one-step look-ahead via emulator (gamma 0), only options from the initial state shown; qualitative trajectory plots.
limits: No reward scores. Myopic policies missed the key in Montezuma. Qualitative only.
agent_relevance: Evidence that SR eigenvectors recover human-style subgoals in a hard-exploration game. It also marks a failure (needs lookahead in Freeway).

source: Machado, Barreto, Precup, Bowling (2023) Temporal Abstraction in RL with the Successor Representation (JMLR 24)
finding: Long JMLR synthesis: the SR is a natural base for discovering, combining and refining options. Frames a loop (representation -> options -> better data -> better representation). Adds the option keyboard to combine learned options into combinatorially many.
numbers: Ten randomly sampled tasks for eigenoption tests plus rooms exploration studies.
limits: Mostly gridworld.
agent_relevance: Gives a design pattern: representation and subgoal library refine each other.

source: Machado, Barreto, Precup, Bowling (2023) Temporal Abstraction in RL with the Successor Representation (JMLR 24)
finding: In ten randomly sampled tasks, as few as four eigenoptions sped up learning and four options never hurt performance. Covering options (Jinnai 2019), surprisingly, did NOT improve performance in these tasks; authors conjecture a sparse initiation set is the cause.
numbers: Ten tasks, appendix D; one representative task shown in the main text.
quote: covering options did not improve the agent's performance. This was consistent across the ten tasks.
limits: Authors say 'conjecture'; not tested further there.
agent_relevance: Contradicts the earlier finding that few eigenoptions hurt, and contradicts Jinnai's claim that covering options are better. Results depend on setup (initiation sets, task).

source: Machado, Barreto, Precup, Bowling (2023) Temporal Abstraction in RL with the Successor Representation (JMLR 24)
finding: Related methods: Stachenfeld et al. use SR eigenvectors for a normalised min-cut (bottleneck states; sign of eigenvector gives partition). Successor options (Ramesh 2019) cluster SR vectors and find bottlenecks more often than eigenoptions (their Fig 5). Kulkarni 2016 used normalised cuts in deep RL.
numbers: Review text, section 10.1.
limits: Second-hand statements about other papers.
agent_relevance: Two ways to use the same SR: smooth directions (eigenoptions) or partitions (cuts, bottlenecks).

source: Klissarov, Machado (2023) Deep Laplacian-based Options for Temporally-Extended Exploration
finding: Deep Laplacian-based Options (DCEO): fully online, pixel-based, learns the Laplacian eigenfunctions by a neural objective while the agent acts. Compared with Counts, RND, DIAYN, epsilon-greedy and DDQN on 3D navigation, nine rooms, maze, Rubik's cube and Montezuma. At least as good as Counts and RND everywhere; largest gap in Maze; DIAYN did not improve on DDQN.
numbers: Pixel tasks; DDQN for navigation, Rainbow for Montezuma; on 3D navigation DCEO was the only method to consistently get positive reward.
limits: Authors did not run the 2-billion-step RND setting.
agent_relevance: Scalable subgoal discovery now works from pixels online. Gains are in sparse-reward exploration, not general performance.

source: Klissarov, Machado (2023) Deep Laplacian-based Options for Temporally-Extended Exploration
finding: Montezuma's Revenge: DCEO reached a score of 2500 in a few million steps. RND at 2 billion steps surpassed DCEO's performance at 200 million steps, which was all DCEO was run for. DCEO also keeps working after environment changes (non-stationary tasks).
numbers: Montezuma on Rainbow base; 200M-step budget for DCEO.
limits: No head-to-head at equal 2B steps.
agent_relevance: Options help early and when the world changes; not shown to beat the best exploration at huge budgets.

source: Jinnai, Park, Machado, Konidaris (2019) Discovering Options for Exploration by Minimizing Cover Time
finding: Covering options: add edges (options) that maximise the algebraic connectivity of the state graph (Fiedler vector), which lowers a bound on expected cover time. Beats eigenoptions in cover time: four-room 672.0 vs 1094.8; 9x9 grid 258.6 vs 460.5 (8 options each); algebraic connectivity 0.065 vs 0.023 four-room and 0.24 vs 0.12 grid.
numbers: Table 1; 8 options each; Q-learning alpha 0.1 gamma 0.95, 100 episodes, 5 runs; domains: 9x9 grid, four-room, Hanoi, Taxi, Parr's maze, race track.
limits: Machado 2023 found covering options did not help in ten tasks. Table cells were read from layout text; check columns before citing.
agent_relevance: Gives a competing, theory-backed subgoal criterion: pick subgoals that join far-apart regions.

source: Jinnai, Park, Machado, Konidaris (2019) Discovering Options for Exploration by Minimizing Cover Time
finding: In accumulated reward, covering options were better than or equal to eigenoptions in all six domains. Adding more options helped, with falling returns for each extra option (concave in edges added).
numbers: Offline options from adjacency matrix (grid, four-room, Hanoi, Taxi) or incidence matrix (Parr's maze, race track); no reward used to build options.
limits: Small tabular domains, 5 runs.
agent_relevance: Diminishing returns: the first few subgoals give most of the gain.

source: Ramesh, Tomar, Ravindran (2019) Successor Options
finding: Successor options: cluster SR vectors and use centroids as option subgoals. Subgoals are 'landmark' states in the middle of well-connected regions, not choke points. Compared with Q-learning and eigenoptions over 5 seeds, 500 random start/end pairs, horizon 100. Subgoals more diverse and spread than eigenoptions.
numbers: Grid worlds (4 grids), Fetch-Reach for deep version; 6 methods including non-uniform and AE sampling schemes.
limits: Read from partial text; numeric returns not extracted.
agent_relevance: A third subgoal type: landmarks. Useful when choke points are not the key structure.

source: Solway et al. (2014) Optimal behavioral hierarchy (PLoS Comput Biol)
finding: Theory: the best hierarchy is the one that minimises the cost of planning in the decomposed space; this equals Bayesian model selection over decompositions. Four human experiments test it. Exp 1 (N=40): learn a town by adjacency, then pick a 'bus stop'. Bottleneck locations were first choices 4.4 times as often as other locations, after chance adjustment.
numbers: Exp 1 N=40; graph with two bottleneck locations; no bird's-eye view given. Several p-values were stripped from the text I read.
limits: Undergraduate samples; small graphs.
agent_relevance: Humans choose choke points as shortcut targets with no hint. Supports a bottleneck-first subgoal in the library.

source: Solway et al. (2014) Optimal behavioral hierarchy (PLoS Comput Biol)
finding: Exp 2 (N=10) and Exp 3 (N=21): people listing the shortest path chose the bottleneck first; response times differed for bottleneck probes. Exp 4 (N=35, Tower of Hanoi): they preferred the route crossing a single region boundary; 17 subjects took it most often vs 7 the opposite way.
numbers: Same graph in Exp 2 and 3; Exp 4 Hanoi state graph with optimal decomposition.
limits: Percentages stripped in the text I read; 10 to 40 participants per study.
agent_relevance: Planning seems to go region first, steps second. A schema can plan at the level of regions before detail.

source: Botvinick, Niv, Barto (2009) Hierarchically organized behavior and its neural foundations (Cognition)
finding: Hierarchical RL in the options framework mapped to prefrontal cortex. Option subgoals get pseudo-reward; prediction errors are computed inside the option and again for the whole option. Names the open question as how new useful routines are found. Two answers: subgoals from bottlenecks seen on rewarded trajectories, or from analysing the problem graph.
numbers: Review; actor-critic implementation of options; cites McGovern 2002, Pickett and Barto 2002, Thrun and Schwartz 1995, Saffran 1996.
limits: Theory paper; mapping to cortex is proposed, not proven.
agent_relevance: The original statement of the subgoal discovery problem for neuroscience. Pseudo-reward is a model of local success signals.

source: Botvinick, Niv, Barto (2009) Hierarchically organized behavior and its neural foundations (Cognition)
finding: Intrinsic motivation as a source of subgoals: unexpected salient events are rewarding and become option subgoals. Linked to dopamine response to novelty and to curiosity theory (Berlyne, White).
numbers: Review text.
limits: Speculative.
agent_relevance: A trigger for subgoal creation: surprising events, not a schedule.

source: Ribas-Fernandes et al. (2011) A neural signature of hierarchical reinforcement learning (Neuron)
finding: Delivery video game (package then house), with jumps that move the subgoal. HRL predicts a pseudo-reward prediction error (PPE) when the subgoal moves away. EEG (N=9, about 190 delivery trials each, a third with the key jump): negativity at Cz, p<0.01, like the feedback-related negativity. fMRI (N=30): activity in dorsal anterior cingulate tracked PPE size, p<0.01 cluster-corrected.
numbers: EEG N=9, 60 min; fMRI N=30 with jumps of varied size; also anterior insula; a follow-up controlled for subgoal distance. The paper has a further fMRI study not extracted here.
limits: Peak was later than the classic FRN. Small EEG sample.
agent_relevance: Brain signals track progress to a subgoal, separate from reward. Supports a progress check per subgoal.

source: Schapiro, Rogers, Cordova, Turk-Browne, Botvinick (2013) Neural representations of events arise from temporal community structure (Nat Neurosci)
finding: Random walks on a graph with community structure: people press to segment at cluster transitions more than elsewhere. Exp 1 (N=30, 35-min exposure): t(29)=2.27, P<0.05; also in Hamiltonian-path blocks t(29)=2.25, P<0.05. Exp 2 (N=10) replicated with one fixed Hamiltonian path per subject and abstract stimuli.
numbers: Cover task: detect rotated images, A' sensitivity 0.901 (Exp 1). Transition probabilities equal within and across clusters, so segmentation is not from local statistics.
limits: Effects are modest (P just below .05); small N in Exp 2.
agent_relevance: People find community boundaries from transition statistics alone, which is the data a graph-cut subgoal finder uses.

source: Schapiro, Rogers, Cordova, Turk-Browne, Botvinick (2013) Neural representations of events arise from temporal community structure (Nat Neurosci)
finding: Exp 3 (fMRI, N=20, A' about 0.87 to 0.89): items in the same community had more similar neural patterns after exposure. A medial prefrontal cluster was negatively correlated with a cluster-boundary regressor (P<0.05 corrected): engaged within an event, off at boundaries.
numbers: Analysis restricted to Hamiltonian paths to remove local statistics.
limits: No behavioural link to planning shown in this paper.
agent_relevance: Neural support for chunking experience by graph community.

source: Momennejad et al. (2017) The successor representation in human reinforcement learning (Nat Hum Behav)
finding: Humans are more sensitive to reward revaluation than to transition revaluation, as an SR learner predicts (pure model-free or pure model-based would not show this asymmetry). Exp 2 (N=88, three-room sequential task): policy revaluation and transition revaluation produced similar switching (contrast p=0.58); reward, transition and policy all beat the no-revaluation control, p<0.0001.
numbers: Exp 2 N=88; four conditions (reward, transition, policy, no revaluation); the starting state was not revisited in the relearning phase.
limits: A hybrid SR plus model-based fit best, so SR alone is not the story. Exp 1 sample not extracted.
agent_relevance: Evidence that humans carry an SR-like cache, the representation eigenoptions rely on.

source: Momennejad (2020) Learning Structures: Predictive Representations, Replay, and Generalization (Curr Opin Behav Sci)
finding: Review: SR approximates the inverse of the graph Laplacian; its eigenvectors tile the state space like grid fields and help partition and chunk experience, find subgoals, and give 'eigen-options'. Entorhinal grid cells may encode a low-dimensional basis for hierarchical planning and subgoals.
numbers: Review. Policy-dependent SR over-represents bottlenecks and goals, so its eigenvectors differ from a random-walk SR (a prediction, not tested).
quote: Eigen-options simplify planning in complex environments into more manageable components.
limits: Review; the grid-cell account is a proposal.
agent_relevance: The theory link named in the subfield brief: SR eigenvectors give subgoals. Policy dependence is a risk: subgoals depend on how the agent has behaved.

source: Pignatelli et al. (2024) Assessing the Zero-Shot Capabilities of LLMs for Action Evaluation in RL (CALM)
finding: CALM: an LLM splits a task into subgoals and judges whether each transition reaches one, giving auxiliary reward (options discovery by language model). Zero-shot test on NetHack/MiniHack annotated by humans: with the subgoal list given, F1 about 0.60 to 0.74; precision high (0.95 to 0.97 for Llama-3), recall low (about 0.49 to 0.50). When the LLM must invent the subgoals, Llama-3-70B reached F1 0.82 but with many false positives (66 FP vs 19 TN) and recall 0.96.
numbers: 171 positive and 85 negative human-labelled transitions; models: Mixtral-8x7B, gemma-1.1-7b, Llama-3-8B and 70B, command-r; cropped vs full observation; one other table shows Llama-3-70B F1 0.16.
limits: Offline annotation test, no RL training result in this version. Scores swing widely with observation format.
agent_relevance: LLMs can propose subgoals and check them, but are too lenient (false positives) when they write the subgoals themselves. Needs code-checked subgoal tests (G2, G3).

source: Liu et al. (2024) World Models with Hints of Large Language Models for Goal Achieving (DLLM)
finding: Dreaming with LLMs (DLLM): LLM hint subgoals add intrinsic reward inside model rollouts. Reported gains over the strongest baseline: +27.7% HomeGrid, +21.1% Crafter, +9.9% Minecraft. Crafter score 26.4 (GPT-4), 24.4 (GPT-3.5) vs 21.8 for Achievement Distillation.
numbers: Baselines: Dynalang, Achievement Distillation. Goal correctness in HomeGrid: 52.55% standard, 61.64% key info, 66.92% full info; context-insensitive goals 24.30%, 18.34%, 18.95%.
limits: Authors' own benchmark; gains depend on observation info supplied.
agent_relevance: LLM subgoals help, but one third to one half of proposed goals are wrong without extra context. Subgoal proposals should be filtered by checks.

source: Sutton, Precup, Singh (1999) Between MDPs and semi-MDPs: options
finding: Defines an option as (initiation set, policy, termination condition) and gives the semi-Markov theory used by all papers above. Not opened; described from how the opened papers use it.
limits: Not opened this session.
agent_relevance: The formal object a subgoal library stores.

source: McGovern and Barto (2001); Simsek and Barto (2004); Menache et al. (2002)
finding: Earlier bottleneck-based subgoal discovery: diverse density on successful trajectories, betweenness centrality, and Q-cut. Cited as the 'top-down' tradition (Machado 2017 section 6) that the Laplacian work contrasts with. Not opened.
limits: Second-hand via opened papers.
agent_relevance: Baselines for a bottleneck library.
